X1.name: Insurance Discount vs Premium Pricing Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenarios. Recruit 400 recreational boaters (200 per scenario) via boating forums and social media. Randomly assign participants to either a "Insurance Discount" group (PLB offered at $560 with a 20% discount from insurance partner) or a "Premium Pricing" group (PLB offered at $700 with no discount). Both groups receive identical product description emphasizing safety essential for remote water activities and regulatory compliance. Participants indicate intent to purchase (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about current safety gear ownership and insurance status.
X1.sample: 400 recreational boaters (200 per group), recruited from boating forums and social media, balanced for age, experience, and insurance status.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary) and maximum willingness to pay (continuous).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be similar across both price points because boaters value safety regardless of price; willingness to pay will be above $700 for both groups.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be significantly higher in the Insurance Discount group than in the Premium Pricing group, and willingness to pay will be lower in the Premium Pricing group.

X1.decision_rule: If the Insurance Discount group shows at least 15 percentage points higher purchase intent than the Premium Pricing group, proceed with insurance partnership strategy (supporting T2). If purchase intent is similar across groups (difference <10 percentage points), proceed with premium pricing strategy (supporting T1).

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for recreational boaters, positioning the 406 MHz PLB as a safety essential for remote water activities and pricing it at a premium (around $700) through marine retailers and direct-to-consumer channels.
final.target_customer: Recreational boaters who operate in remote waters and value personal safety.
final.value_proposition: A compliant, reliable PLB that addresses a safety gap left by VHF radios and cell phones, offering peace of mind and meeting regulatory requirements for distress signaling.
final.next_action: Conduct the proposed Insurance Discount vs Premium Pricing Test (400 boaters, 10 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent across price points and assess insurance partnership potential.
final.uncertainty: Actual purchase intent and willingness to pay at premium price; insurance companies' willingness to subsidize or require PLBs; competitive response from existing PLB manufacturers.
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent is similar across price points (difference <10 percentage points), confirming T1 and supporting premium pricing.
If the test shows a ≥15 percentage point higher intent in the discount group, indicating T2 and suggesting insurance partnership as primary channel.
If new evidence emerges of strong insurance mandates or subsidies for PLBs in 2002.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment (e.g., market demand, competitive landscape, regulatory requirements, or existing consumer adoption).
Cannot rely on post‑2002 developments or later market outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., personal marine safety beacon for recreational boaters).

4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Form partnerships with consumer brands to co‑brand a consumer‑focused beacon.

ACR can reach boaters through marine retail channels.
predictions: If offered a differentiated PLB, at least 10% of surveyed boaters would express intent to purchase within 12 months.
Sales would be concentrated in coastal states with high boater density.

X1.name: Boater Willingness-to-Pay Survey with Insurance Subsidy Option
X1.method: Online survey of U.S. recreational boaters (coastal states) presenting two scenarios: (1) a differentiated 406 MHz PLB marketed as a safety essential for remote boating, priced at $700; (2) the same PLB offered through marine insurance partners with a subsidy that reduces the effective price to $400 (e.g., insurer covers $300). Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay. The survey also asks about insurance coverage status and whether they would require a PLB as a condition of coverage.
X1.sample: 500 recreational boaters recruited via boating forums and marine retailer email lists, stratified by state (California, Florida, Washington, Texas) to reflect high boater density. Randomly assigned to either the premium-pricing scenario or the insurance-subsidy scenario (250 each).
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying "yes") and average maximum price willing to pay (in dollars).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be at least 10% in the premium-pricing scenario and will not increase significantly when the price is reduced to $400 (i.e., <5 percentage point difference).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be at least 15% in the insurance-subsidy scenario and will be at least 5 percentage points higher than in the premium-pricing scenario.

X1.decision_rule: If the insurance-subsidy scenario yields a purchase intent rate ≥15% and is at least 5 percentage points higher than the premium-pricing scenario, proceed to develop a consumer proposition leveraging insurance partnerships. If the premium-pricing scenario yields ≥10% and the price reduction does not significantly increase intent, proceed with a premium

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition for recreational boaters, positioning the 406 MHz PLB as a safety essential for remote boating. Use premium pricing (~$700) and sell through specialty marine retailers. Begin with a limited launch in high‑boater states (California, Florida, Washington, Texas) to test demand before broader rollout.
final.target_customer: Recreational boaters in coastal U.S. states who engage in remote boating activities.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated 406 MHz PLB marketed as a critical safety device for remote boating, leveraging FCC approval and ACR's safety heritage to justify premium pricing and capture higher margins than bulk B2B sales.
final.next_action: Run the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (500 boaters, two pricing scenarios) within the 12‑week test window to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before committing to full product development.
final.uncertainty: Demand for a premium-priced PLB among recreational boaters is uncertain; willingness to pay $700 and adoption rates are unknown. Insurance subsidy mechanisms (T2) remain untested and could alter the optimal go-to-market approach.
would_change_if: If the survey shows purchase intent <10% in the premium scenario or a >5‑percentage‑point increase when price is reduced to $400, reconsider premium positioning and explore insurance partnership or lower‑price strategy.
If new evidence shows insurers actively subsidizing PLBs or requiring them as a condition of coverage, shift focus to T2 and develop an insurance‑channel distribution model.

X1.name: Marine Retailer Willingness-to-Pay Survey
X1.method: Online survey of recreational boaters who own boats over 15 feet and have taken safety courses. Participants are shown a mock product description of ACR's 406 MHz PLB (GPS-enabled, marine-certified, $700 retail price) and asked: "Would you purchase this beacon for your boat?" and "What is the maximum price you would pay?". A second group sees the same description but with a note that "insurance companies may offer premium discounts for beacon owners" and is asked the same questions. The survey also asks about current safety equipment ownership and insurance premium sensitivity.
X1.sample: 300 boaters recruited via boating forums and marine retailer email lists, stratified by region (East Coast, Gulf, West Coast).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be high (≥40%) and WTP will be at or above $700, indicating boaters view the beacon as a safety necessity and are willing to pay premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be lower without insurance note (≤30%) but will increase significantly (≥50%) when insurance discount is mentioned, and WTP will drop to around $500, indicating demand is driven by insurance incentives.

X1.decision_rule: If purchase intent with insurance note is ≥50% and WTP ≤$500, proceed with insurance partnership strategy (support T2). If purchase intent without insurance note is ≥40% and WTP ≥$700, proceed with direct premium consumer launch (support T1). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

final.next_action: Conduct the proposed Marine Retailer Willingness-to-Pay Survey (10 weeks, €15,000) to validate purchase intent and price sensitivity before full launch.

arguments.why_behaviour_changes: Regulatory approval for land-based use and FCC certification for marine use create a legal pathway for boaters to use PLBs. Boaters perceive remote water activities as high-risk and seek reliable distress signaling. A differentiated product

arguments.name: Marine Retailer Willingness-to-Pay Survey
arguments.method: Online survey of recreational boaters who own boats over 15 feet and have taken safety courses. Participants are shown a mock product description of ACR's 406 MHz PLB (GPS-enabled, marine-certified, $700 retail price) and asked: "Would you purchase this beacon for your boat?" and "What is the maximum price you would pay?". A second group sees the same description but with a note that "insurance companies may offer premium discounts for beacon owners" and is asked the same questions. The survey also asks about current safety equipment ownership and insurance premium sensitivity.
arguments.sample: 300 boaters recruited via boating forums and marine retailer email lists, stratified by region (East Coast, Gulf, West Coast).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Purchase intent will be high (≥40%) and WTP will be at or above $700, indicating boaters view the beacon as a safety necessity and are willing to pay premium.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Purchase intent will be lower without insurance note (≤30%) but will increase significantly (≥50%) when insurance discount is mentioned, and WTP will drop to around $500, indicating demand is driven by insurance incentives.

arguments.decision_rule: If purchase intent with insurance note is ≥50% and WTP ≤$500, proceed with insurance partnership strategy (support T2). If purchase intent without insurance note is ≥40% and WTP ≥$700, proceed with direct premium consumer launch (support T1). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting recreational boaters, emphasizing the beacon as a safety necessity with premium pricing, while also exploring insurance partnerships as a secondary channel.

frame.objective: Determine whether ACR Electronics should invest in developing a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case based on its 406 MHz satellite distress-beacon technology, using evidence available up to late 2002.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before late 2002; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence that justifies the investment (e.g., market demand, competitive landscape, regulatory requirements, or existing consumer adoption).
Cannot rely on post‑2002 developments or later market outcomes.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer product for a specific use case (e.g., personal marine safety beacon for recreational boaters).
2) Expand into adjacent consumer segments without differentiation (e.g., sell existing 406 MHz beacons through retail channels to individual buyers).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on existing B2B markets (ships, aircraft, military/commercial marine).
4) License the 406 MHz technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Form partnerships with consumer brands to co‑brand a consumer‑focused beacon.

X1.name: Consumer Willingness-to-Pay Test for Differentiated PLB
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase scenario. Participants are shown a product description of a differentiated 406 MHz PLB (GPS integration, retail price $700) and asked to indicate the maximum price they would pay and whether they would purchase it. The survey also asks about peer influence: "How much would you be influenced if friends in your boating/camping group owned this device?" (1‑10 scale).
X1.sample: 200 recreational boaters and outdoor enthusiasts recruited via boating clubs, camping forums, and outdoor retailer email lists. Stratified to ensure geographic diversity (US coastal states).
X1.measure: 1) Average willingness-to-pay (WTP) in dollars. 2) Purchase intent (binary: would buy at $700). 3) Peer influence score (average of 1‑10 responses).

prediction_by_theory.T1: WTP will be high (>= $700) and purchase intent will be driven by perceived safety necessity, independent of peer influence. Peer influence score will not significantly predict purchase intent.
prediction_by_theory.T2: WTP will be lower than $700 on average, but purchase intent will increase significantly when peer influence is high (e.g., top quartile of peer influence scores). Peer influence will be a stronger predictor of purchase than safety necessity.

X1.decision_rule: If average WTP >= $700 AND purchase intent >= 30% AND peer influence does NOT significantly predict purchase intent (p > 0.05), then T1 is supported and we recommend developing a differentiated consumer product. If average WTP < $700 OR purchase intent < 20% OR peer influence significantly predicts purchase (p < 0.05), then T2 is more likely and we recommend focusing on community/partnership approach rather than premium pricing.

revisions.reason: Simulated evidence SYN-D concerns warehouse packing efficiency and does not address consumer demand, pricing, or peer influence mechanisms central to T1. Therefore it does not affect the theory.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for recreational boaters and outdoor enthusiasts, positioning the 406 MHz PLB as a premium safety necessity with GPS integration, priced around $700, and sold through specialty outdoor retailers.
final.target_customer: Recreational boaters and outdoor enthusiasts who engage in remote activities where traditional communication fails.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated 406 MHz PLB that integrates GPS, meets FCC certification for land-based use, and is marketed as a personal safety product, allowing premium pricing and brand building around safety.
final.next_action: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (200 participants, 10 weeks, €15,000) to test price sensitivity and peer influence effects before full product development.
final.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains about actual consumer willingness to pay premium prices and the strength of peer influence versus safety necessity as purchase drivers. The test will resolve this.
would_change_if: If the survey shows average willingness-to-pay below $700 or purchase intent below 20%, we would reconsider the premium positioning and explore lower-price or partnership models.
If peer influence emerges as the primary driver (significant predictor of purchase), we would shift focus to community/partnership strategies rather than premium retail.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting households with small gardens, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network and engineering. The evidence shows rapid growth in garden tractor demand driven by price‑sensitive, practical needs of small‑garden households, and Deere already has a dealer infrastructure to reach them.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell garden tractors through its existing dealer network at premium prices justified by brand reputation and engineering quality, generating additional revenue streams.

X1.name: Targeted Purchase Intent Survey
X1.method: Online survey with targeted recruitment of two distinct groups: (1) households with small gardens (≤0.5 acres) and (2) professional landscapers/small‑farm operators (≤50 acres). Participants view a mock Deere garden tractor (based on 1963 110 model) with price options: $400 (budget) and $600 (premium). They indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and willingness to pay. The survey also asks about primary use case (home garden vs. professional work).
X1.sample: 200 respondents: 100 from each group, recruited via regional agricultural extension services and landscaping associations. Stratify by state to reflect 1960s demographic distribution.
X1.measure: Purchase intent rate (percentage saying "yes") for each price point, and average willingness to pay (WTP) in dollars.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Households with small gardens will show higher purchase intent at the $400 price point than professionals, and overall WTP will be lower, reflecting price sensitivity.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Professionals will show higher purchase intent at the $600 price point than households, and overall WTP will be higher, reflecting willingness to pay for reliability.

The evidence shows rapid growth in garden tractor demand driven by price‑sensitive, practical needs of small‑garden households, and Deere already has a dealer infrastructure to reach them.

final.value_proposition: A Deere garden tractor positioned as an affordable, reliable, and easy‑to‑use solution for yard chores, sold through existing dealers at a price point reflecting the "inexpensive, practical, economical" attributes noted in independent
final.next_action: Conduct the proposed Targeted Purchase Intent Survey (200 respondents, 10 weeks, €18,000) to validate demand and price sensitivity before full investment.
final.uncertainty: The size of the small‑garden market and its willingness to pay a premium for Deere branding remain uncertain; professional demand is also unknown.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering reputation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; garden tractors offer a cost‑effective solution for yard work compared to manual labor or larger equipment.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and reliability to justify higher margins.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach individual consumers without major new infrastructure.
Consumers perceive Deere tractors as reliable and are willing to pay a premium for the brand.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor line, sales will increase among households with small gardens within 12 months.
Dealers will report higher profit margins on garden tractor sales compared to traditional farm equipment.
Consumer surveys will show that price sensitivity is lower for Deere tractors than for generic brands.
T1.first_claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they are inexpensive, practical for chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T2.claim: Deere's existing dealer network will drive consumer adoption of garden tractors because dealers already serve individual buyers and can cross‑sell tractors as add‑ons to farm equipment, creating a low‑cost distribution channel.
T2.who_benefits: Deere benefits by utilizing its established dealer infrastructure to reach consumers without building new sales channels, capturing additional revenue from a new product line.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Dealers are motivated to sell garden tractors because they increase overall store traffic and profit margins, and they already have relationships with small‑farm owners who may need both farm and garden equipment.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can price garden tractors at a premium while leveraging dealer relationships to move units, and can bundle attachments to increase average transaction value.
assumptions: Dealers are willing to allocate shelf space and promotional effort to garden tractors.
Small‑farm owners purchase both farm and garden equipment from the same dealer.
Deere can produce garden tractors at a cost that allows dealers a reasonable margin.
predictions: If Deere introduces garden tractors, dealer sales of garden tractors will rise within 12 months.
Dealers will report higher overall profit per customer when selling garden tractors compared to selling only farm equipment.
Consumer surveys will show that dealers are a primary source of information for garden tractor purchases.

position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition targeting households with small gardens, leveraging Deere’s existing dealer network to sell garden tractors and attachments. Use the proposed Dealer Preference Test to validate dealer willingness and pricing before full rollout.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Must identify evidence of consumer demand, market size, competitive landscape, and feasibility of adapting tractor technology to a consumer use case.
Must consider Deere’s existing dealer network and its current reach to individual buyers.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
3) No expansion: continue focusing on the current farm and industrial equipment market.
4) License Deere’s tractor technology to third‑party manufacturers for consumer applications.
5) Create a new brand or sub‑brand targeting a different customer segment (e.g., urban gardeners) while retaining the core farm business.

T1.claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for various chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.
T1.who_benefits: Deere & Company would benefit by capturing sales of lawn and garden tractors through its existing dealer network, leveraging its engineering reputation.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Rising homeownership and suburban growth increase the number of households with small gardens; these households seek affordable, versatile tools for yard work.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere can sell tractors and attachments through its dealer network at premium prices, using its brand reputation for quality and reliability.
assumptions: Homeownership rates continue to rise in the 1960s, expanding the pool of potential buyers.
Small garden owners prioritize cost-effectiveness and ease of use over brand prestige.
Deere's dealer network can be leveraged to reach these consumers without major new investment.
predictions: If Deere launches a differentiated garden tractor proposition, sales will increase among households with small gardens.
Surveyed garden owners will indicate willingness to pay a premium for a Deere-branded tractor due to perceived quality and dealer support.
T1.first_claim: Households with small gardens will adopt garden tractors because they find them inexpensive, practical for various chores, and economical to maintain, creating demand for a differentiated consumer proposition.

T2.claim: Deere's existing dealer network will reach individual buyers because the network already serves small farm owners who also need garden tractors, creating a natural cross‑sell opportunity without new marketing.
T2.who_benefits: Deere benefits by increasing sales of garden tractors through existing dealer relationships, reducing customer acquisition cost.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Small farm owners already purchase Deere equipment for farming; they also maintain gardens and seek convenient, trusted sources for garden tools.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere can bundle garden tractors with farm equipment or sell them as add‑ons through dealers, capturing additional revenue from existing customers.
assumptions: Small farm owners have significant garden space requiring machinery.
Deere dealers are willing to stock and promote garden tractors to their farming customers.
Farm owners prioritize convenience and trust in their existing dealer over brand or price differences.
predictions: If Deere offers garden tractors through its dealer network, farm owners will purchase them at higher rates than if sold through new channels.
Dealers will report increased sales of garden tractors when offered as add‑ons to farm equipment purchases.

X1.name: Dealer Preference Test
X1.method: Survey Deere dealers about their willingness to stock and promote garden tractors to two distinct customer segments: (1) small garden households (identified by property size < 1 acre and no farm equipment purchase in past year) and (2) small farm owners (identified by farm equipment purchase in past year). Dealers will be offered a hypothetical commission structure: a flat 10% on garden tractor sales, with an additional 5% bonus if the sale is to a small farm owner. They will indicate (a) whether they would stock the product, (b) the minimum price they would accept, and (c) the likelihood of recommending it to each segment on a 1‑10 scale.
X1.sample: 100 Deere dealers (estimated 10% of total dealer network) recruited via existing dealer list. Stratify by region to ensure geographic diversity.
X1.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of dealers willing to stock garden tractors for each segment. Secondary outcomes: average minimum price accepted and recommendation likelihood scores.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher willingness to stock and lower minimum price for small garden households, because demand is driven by household need and cost‑effectiveness.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher willingness to stock and higher minimum price for small farm owners, because dealers already serve this segment and see cross‑sell opportunity.

arguments.name: Dealer Preference Test
arguments.method: Survey Deere dealers about their willingness to stock and promote garden tractors to two distinct customer segments: (1) small garden households (identified by property size < 1 acre and no farm equipment purchase in past year) and (2) small farm owners (identified by farm equipment purchase in past year). Dealers will be offered a hypothetical commission structure: a flat 10% on garden tractor sales, with an additional 5% bonus if the sale is to a small farm owner. They will indicate (a) whether they would stock the product, (b) the minimum price they would accept, and (c) the likelihood of recommending it to each segment on a 1‑10 scale.
arguments.sample: 100 Deere dealers (estimated 10% of total dealer network) recruited via existing dealer list. Stratify by region to ensure geographic diversity.
arguments.measure: Primary outcome: proportion of dealers willing to stock garden tractors for each segment. Secondary outcomes: average minimum price accepted and recommendation likelihood scores.

prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher willingness to stock and higher minimum price for small farm owners, because dealers already serve this segment and see cross‑sell opportunity.

frame.objective: Determine whether Deere & Company should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case that leverages its tractor engineering, based on evidence available in mid-1962.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., small‑farm or hobbyist tractor) using Deere’s engineering.
2) Expand the existing dealer network to reach more individual buyers without a differentiated proposition (e.g., marketing tractors directly to smallholders).
